questions.stem: Which factor most often explains why an introduced species becomes far more abundant in Australia than in its native range?
options: It experiences a harsher climate that slows its rate of reproduction
It has left behind the predators, parasites and diseases that limited it at home
It has evolved a larger body size during the voyage to its new environment
It meets native competitors that are better adapted than those in its home range
questions.explanation: In a new region an introduced species often escapes the natural enemies that kept its numbers in check, so environmental resistance is lower. Meeting stronger competitors or a harsher climate would limit it, not help it.

questions.stem: Which combination of traits makes an introduced plant most likely to become invasive in Tasmania?
options: Slow growth, a few large seeds and dependence on one specialist pollinator
A long juvenile period, short-lived seed and a very narrow tolerance of soil types
Shallow roots, poor dispersal and a need for frequent heavy pruning to flower
Rapid growth, abundant long-lived seed and tolerance of a wide range of conditions
questions.explanation: Invasive species are typically generalists that grow and reproduce quickly, build up large seed banks and tolerate varied conditions, so they establish and spread easily. Specialist, slow-reproducing species rarely become invasive.

questions.stem: Gorse, a spiny European shrub, forms dense infestations along Tasmanian roadsides and cleared farmland but rarely invades intact wet forest. What does this pattern suggest?
options: Roads release chemicals that gorse needs to germinate, and these chemicals are absent from the forest
Disturbed, open sites give introduced species light and space that intact native vegetation does not
Gorse can grow only where native plants are present, because it depends on their roots for nutrients
Intact wet forest is too dry for gorse, so it survives only where farmers irrigate the soil
questions.explanation: Clearing, roads and grazing create open, disturbed ground with high light and little competition, which suits many weeds. Intact native vegetation offers fewer gaps. Wet forest is not too dry for gorse; it is too shady and crowded.

questions.stem: The northern Pacific seastar is established in Tasmania's Derwent estuary. Which human activity is the most likely pathway for marine pests such as this to reach new ports?
options: Deliberate release by fishers seeking to improve local catches
Natural migration of adults swimming across open oceans
Seabirds carrying adult seastars long distances in their beaks
Ballast water and hull fouling on ships moving between ports
questions.explanation: Larvae and small organisms are carried in ships' ballast water or attached to hulls, then released or dislodged in a new port. Adult seastars cannot cross open oceans on their own, and they were not introduced deliberately.

questions.stem: Japanese kelp (Undaria pinnatifida) was first recorded in Australia in 1988 on Tasmania's east coast. It is classed as an introduced species because:
options: it is a native species that has become more common in warm years
people carried it from its native range in the north-west Pacific
it evolved recently from native kelp off the Tasmanian coast
it spread south naturally on warm currents from tropical Australia
questions.explanation: An introduced species is one moved by human activity outside its natural range. Undaria is native to the north-west Pacific and is thought to have arrived with shipping. A native species spreading naturally would not be classed as introduced.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an introduced species harming native species by predation?
options: Gorse shading out native shrubs along roadside verges
Introduced honeybees occupying tree hollows used by parrots
Feral cats killing small native mammals, birds and reptiles
Rabbits eating native seedlings and grasses in the Midlands
questions.explanation: Predation means killing and eating other animals, as feral cats do to small native wildlife. Rabbits are herbivores that compete with native grazers and damage vegetation, and gorse and honeybees compete for light and hollows.

questions.stem: Introduced honeybees often occupy tree hollows that native parrots and possums need for nesting. This impact is best described as:
options: interspecific competition for a limited resource
predation on native species by an introduced animal
parasitism of native species by an introduced insect
mutualism between an introduced and a native species
questions.explanation: When two different species use the same limited resource, here hollows, they compete. The bees do not eat or feed on the birds and mammals, so it is not predation or parasitism.

questions.stem: Phytophthora cinnamomi, an introduced soil-borne pathogen, causes dieback in Tasmanian heath and buttongrass moorland. Silver banksia disappears from infested moorland while buttongrass survives. What is the main effect on the ecosystem?
options: Buttongrass spreads the pathogen to animals, causing disease in native mammals and birds
The pathogen adds nitrogen to the soil, so faster-growing native plants replace the banksia
Species composition changes as susceptible plants die, reducing diversity and habitat for animals
All plant species die equally, so the moorland becomes bare ground within a single growing season
questions.explanation: Phytophthora kills susceptible species such as silver banksia while resistant species like buttongrass persist, so the community becomes simpler and loses food and shelter for animals. It affects plants, not animals, and it kills selectively rather than equally.

questions.stem: Rabbits and introduced grazers remove ground cover from hillsides in eastern Tasmania. Which chain of effects is most likely?
options: Bare soil cools down, frost becomes rare and native grasses grow through winter
Bare soil erodes in heavy rain, sediment enters streams and aquatic habitat is degraded
Bare soil absorbs more rain, groundwater rises and streams flow more strongly in summer
Bare soil traps more nutrients, native shrubs grow faster and erosion stops completely
questions.explanation: Without plant cover, rain detaches and washes away soil, which ends up as sediment in streams, smothering habitat and reducing water quality. This is habitat degradation by an introduced species. Bare soil absorbs less rain, not more.

questions.stem: Japanese kelp has spread along parts of Tasmania's east coast, by one estimate at about 10 km per year. Surveys at invaded sites show fewer native seaweed species. Which conclusion is best supported, and what further evidence would strengthen it?
options: It definitely causes the decline; no further evidence is needed because the pattern across the sites is so clear
Native seaweeds are declining for other reasons; Japanese kelp only ever spreads into areas left empty
It is beneficial; the native seaweed decline shows that diversity was too high before the invasion
It may be outcompeting native seaweeds; surveys of matched invaded and uninvaded sites over time would test this
questions.explanation: A correlation between invasion and fewer native species suggests competition, but other factors could be involved. Comparing invaded and uninvaded sites, or before-and-after surveys with controls, would strengthen the causal link. Claiming certainty from a pattern alone overstates the evidence.

questions.stem: Introduced species can spread disease to native wildlife. Which example fits this impact?
options: Gorse thickets providing dense cover where foxes and feral cats can shelter and breed
Willows along rivers dropping all their leaves into streams in autumn
Carp stirring up sediment so that the water becomes cloudy
Domestic and feral cats spreading the parasite Toxoplasma to native marsupials
questions.explanation: Cats are the definitive host of Toxoplasma gondii, which can infect and kill native marsupials. The other options are habitat changes, not disease transmission.

questions.stem: Divers removing northern Pacific seastars by hand from a marina is an example of which control method?
options: Manual removal
Biological control
Chemical control
Exclusion fencing
questions.explanation: Physically collecting and removing pest organisms is manual removal. Biological control uses a living natural enemy, and chemical control uses poisons.

questions.stem: Biological control of an introduced pest involves:
options: spraying a selective herbicide or insecticide that targets only the pest species
trapping and shooting the pest across its whole range in the wild
introducing a native competitor that has been bred in captivity
releasing a natural enemy of the pest, such as a predator, parasite or disease
questions.explanation: Biological control uses living organisms, usually from the pest's home range, that attack the pest. Herbicides and insecticides are chemical control, and trapping and shooting are physical methods.

questions.stem: The gorse spider mite was released in Tasmania from 1998 and is now established on gorse throughout the state. It damages gorse foliage but rarely kills bushes. What does this suggest about biological control?
options: It fails whenever the pest survives, so the mite release achieved nothing
It works only on animals, so plant pests cannot be targeted by insects or mites
It usually reduces a pest's vigour and spread over time rather than eradicating it
It always eradicates a pest completely within a few years of the agent's first release
questions.explanation: Biological control is a long-term strategy that aims to reduce a pest's growth, seed output and spread, and agents rarely eliminate a pest completely. Weakened gorse is easier to manage with other methods, so a partial effect is still useful.

questions.stem: A biological control agent reduced a pest mammal population by about 90% within three years of its release. Ten years later, the pest's numbers have partly recovered even though the agent is still present. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Each pest animal learned to resist the agent after infection and passed this learning to its offspring
The agent was successful, so the recovery must be due to a sampling error in the later surveys
The agent evolved to attack native species instead, and so it stopped affecting the pest altogether
Individuals with inherited resistance survived and bred, so resistance became more common in the population
questions.explanation: Strong selection by a disease favours individuals with inherited resistance, which survive and pass on their alleles, so the population becomes more resistant over generations. Acquired immunity or learning is not inherited. This is why biological control often needs new strains or agents over time.

questions.stem: Before a new biological control agent is approved for release in Australia, it must pass host-specificity testing. What is the main purpose of this testing?
options: To show the agent reproduces faster than the pest it is meant to control
To show the agent can be eradicated easily if it fails to establish
To show the agent will attack only the target pest and not native or crop species
To show the agent can survive in every climate zone of the Australian continent
questions.explanation: The main risk of biological control is that the agent attacks non-target species, as cane toads did. Host-specificity testing exposes the agent to related native and crop plants or animals to check it attacks only the target.

questions.stem: Rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus was being tested on Wardang Island in South Australia when it escaped in 1995 and spread rapidly across Australia. Which issue does this event best illustrate?
options: Biological control agents always fail on islands because island populations have no genetic variation
Biological control agents harm only the target species, so their escape never raises any concerns
Biological control agents can spread beyond planned areas, so release cannot always be controlled
Biological control agents cannot spread on their own, so they must be released by hand at every site
questions.explanation: The virus left the trial site and reached distant parts of Australia within months, before a planned release. A living agent can disperse by itself, which is both its strength and a risk. The escape was concerning precisely because spread could not be controlled.

questions.stem: Many Tasmanian councils use herbicide to control willows along rivers. Why is spraying near waterways handled with particular care?
options: Chemicals can drift or wash into the water and harm non-target plants and aquatic animals
Herbicides become stronger in water and turn the willows into a more invasive, faster-growing form
Rivers dilute herbicides completely, so spraying near water has no effect on willows
Willows near water cannot absorb herbicide, so spraying them only wastes chemicals
questions.explanation: A drawback of chemical control is harm to non-target organisms. Near water, spray drift or runoff can affect native plants, invertebrates and fish. Herbicides do not make a plant more invasive.

questions.stem: A land manager must choose a control method for a small, newly found patch of an invasive weed in a reserve. Which choice is best, and why?
options: Manual removal now, because a small, isolated infestation can be eradicated before it spreads
Biological control later, because releasing an agent suits a small, isolated patch of weed best
No action, because new weeds usually die out on their own in an unfamiliar environment
Burning the whole reserve, because fire kills weeds while native plants are unaffected
questions.explanation: Eradication is most likely when an infestation is small and caught early, and hand removal is targeted and cheap at that scale. Biological control suits widespread pests where eradication is no longer feasible. Burning a whole reserve would damage native vegetation too.

questions.stem: A walking track runs from moorland infested with Phytophthora cinnamomi into an uninfested area. Where should a boot washdown station be placed to best protect the uninfested area?
options: Where walkers leave the infested area, before they enter the uninfested moorland
At the far end of the uninfested area, after walkers have crossed all of it
In the middle of the infested area, so walkers clean boots while still inside it
At the car park only, because spores cannot move once walkers are on the track
questions.explanation: Phytophthora spreads in soil and mud carried on boots, vehicles and equipment. Cleaning boots on leaving the infested area, before entering clean ground, stops spores being carried in. Cleaning after crossing the uninfested area would be too late.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares two pest animal control methods?
options: Poison baiting can treat large areas cheaply but risks killing non-target animals that eat the bait
Shooting can treat large areas cheaply and has no effect on either animal welfare or on public safety
Trapping kills every pest in an area, so populations never recover once trapping stops
Poison baiting is completely selective, so only the target pest can ever be affected
questions.explanation: Baiting covers large areas efficiently, but non-target species may take baits, so bait type and placement must be managed. Shooting is labour intensive and raises welfare and safety issues, and no method removes every animal.

questions.stem: Foxes are not established in Tasmania, and several mammals that disappeared from much of the mainland, such as the eastern quoll, still live there. What does this suggest about managing introduced predators?
options: Eastern quolls are not affected by any predators, so their mainland disappearance is unrelated to foxes
Tasmania should introduce foxes, because native mammals would then evolve defences more quickly
Preventing a predator from establishing can protect species that would otherwise decline, so early detection matters
Introduced predators have little effect on mammals, so the quoll's survival there must be due to the mild climate alone
questions.explanation: Foxes are widely linked to mainland mammal declines, and Tasmania's lack of an established fox population has made it a refuge. This shows the value of biosecurity and rapid response. It does not mean predators are irrelevant; feral cats still threaten Tasmanian wildlife.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of genetic diversity?
options: Variation in the alleles carried by individuals within a population of eastern quolls
The number of different bird species recorded in a patch of wet sclerophyll forest
The range of ecosystems from alpine heath to estuaries in a single river catchment
The number of individual Tasmanian devils counted along a survey route each night
questions.explanation: Genetic diversity is the variety of genes and alleles within a species or population. The number of species is species diversity, the range of habitats is ecosystem diversity, and a count of individuals measures abundance.

questions.stem: Species diversity takes into account:
options: only the total number of individual organisms found in a given area
only the variety of different habitats found in a region
the number of alleles found in one species across its whole range
both the number of species and how evenly individuals are spread among them
questions.explanation: Species diversity combines species richness, the number of species, with evenness, how equally individuals are distributed among them. A count of individuals alone measures abundance, not diversity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes ecosystem diversity in Tasmania?
options: The variety of habitats and communities, from rainforest and moorland to estuaries and kelp reefs
The number of different eucalypt species found growing together in a single small patch of dry forest
The range of alleles within the Tasmanian devil population across the island
The total number of animals living in the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area
questions.explanation: Ecosystem diversity is the variety of different ecosystems, each with its own community and abiotic conditions. The number of eucalypt species in one patch is species diversity, and alleles within devils is genetic diversity.

questions.stem: Tasmanian devils have very low genetic diversity, which predates devil facial tumour disease. How might this have contributed to the disease's spread?
options: Low genetic diversity makes devils breed faster, so the disease spreads through a larger number of young animals
Low genetic diversity makes devils less aggressive, so they bite each other more often when feeding
Low genetic diversity means devils have no immune system, so any disease can infect them easily
Tumour cells from one devil are less likely to be recognised as foreign by another devil's immune system
questions.explanation: Devil facial tumour disease spreads as living cancer cells passed by biting. Because devils are genetically similar, their immune systems are less likely to reject cells from another devil as foreign. Devils do have immune systems; the issue is reduced variation.

questions.stem: Why is genetic diversity within a crop's wild relatives valuable to agriculture?
options: It provides alleles for traits such as drought or disease resistance that breeders can use
It ensures that every crop plant is identical, which makes harvesting more efficient
It prevents the crop from ever hybridising with weeds growing in nearby paddocks
It reduces the need for pollinators because genetically varied plants self-fertilise
questions.explanation: Wild relatives carry alleles that may have been lost from cultivated varieties, which breeders can use to develop crops that resist new pests, diseases or climates. Genetically identical crops are more vulnerable, not less.

questions.stem: Why does high species diversity tend to make an ecosystem more resilient?
options: Several species can perform similar roles, so losing one does not stop key processes
Each species competes with all others, so populations stay small and never change
More species means less energy is lost at each trophic level of the food chain
Diverse ecosystems contain no predators, so prey populations are always stable
questions.explanation: With many species, functions such as pollination, decomposition and predation are often shared, so the ecosystem keeps working if one species declines. Species diversity does not change the energy lost between trophic levels.

questions.stem: Which is the best reason to conserve ecosystem diversity, not just individual species?
options: Each ecosystem supports its own community and services, so losing one can remove many species at once
Ecosystems are easy to recreate, so conserving them costs less than protecting individual species
Individual species never depend on their habitat, so protecting whole ecosystems is mainly about scenery
Ecosystem diversity guarantees that no species in any ecosystem can ever become extinct
questions.explanation: Each ecosystem supports its own community and provides services such as water filtration or coastal protection. Losing an ecosystem, such as lowland grassland, removes the many species that depend on it. Ecosystems are very hard to recreate once lost.

questions.stem: A seed bank stores seed from a single population of a threatened Tasmanian plant. A second proposal would collect seed from all eight remaining populations. Which reason best supports the second proposal?
options: Sampling all populations ensures every stored seed will germinate when it is planted
Sampling all populations prevents the species from ever hybridising with other plants in the future
Sampling all populations captures more of the species' genetic diversity for future restoration
Sampling all populations increases the number of species stored in the seed bank
questions.explanation: Different populations carry different alleles, so collecting across the range conserves more genetic diversity, giving restored populations a better chance to adapt. It does not add species or guarantee germination.

questions.stem: Which is generally regarded as the greatest threat to biodiversity in Australia?
options: Habitat destruction and degradation, such as land clearing
Collection of native plants for gardens by hobbyists
Hunting of native birds for food by recreational shooters
Natural volcanic eruptions on the Australian mainland
questions.explanation: Clearing and degradation of habitat remove the food, shelter and breeding sites species need, and are a leading cause of decline across Australia. Collecting and hunting affect particular species but are smaller threats overall.

questions.stem: Clearing for agriculture has left Tasmania's lowland native grasslands as small, scattered remnants. Which problem does fragmentation cause for the species living in them?
options: Remnants have less edge, so weeds and predators find it harder to enter them
Remnants always contain more species than the original continuous grassland did
Small isolated populations lose genetic diversity and are more easily wiped out by chance events
Small isolated populations gain genetic diversity because they mate with more distant relatives
questions.explanation: Fragmentation splits habitat into small patches, so populations become small and isolated. They lose genetic diversity through inbreeding and drift, and fire, drought or disease can wipe out a whole patch. Small remnants have more edge relative to area, not less.

questions.stem: Warming waters off eastern Tasmania have allowed the long-spined sea urchin to extend its range south from New South Wales and graze kelp reefs into barrens. This is an example of which threatening process?
options: Climate change altering species distributions and ecosystems
Pollution from industrial discharges into estuaries
Overharvesting of a species for commercial sale
Habitat clearing for urban and agricultural land
questions.explanation: The urchin is a native Australian species whose range has shifted south as warming and a stronger East Australian Current changed conditions. This is a climate-driven change, not pollution or clearing.

questions.stem: Mercury and other heavy metals in an estuary can harm biodiversity mainly because they:
options: accumulate in organisms and become more concentrated at higher trophic levels
dissolve quickly and become harmless once they are diluted in seawater
are used by plankton as nutrients, causing algal blooms and eutrophication
are broken down by bacteria into oxygen, raising dissolved oxygen levels
questions.explanation: Heavy metals are persistent and are not easily excreted, so they bioaccumulate in organisms and biomagnify up food chains, harming top predators. They do not become harmless when diluted.

questions.stem: A survey of a remnant woodland finds that native ground-nesting birds declined after a road was built nearby. Feral cat sightings, weed cover and road-killed animals all increased. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: The road must have improved the habitat, because more animals were seen near it
Several threatening processes are acting together, so management should address more than one
Feral cats alone caused the decline, so cat control is the only management action that would help
Weeds are irrelevant to birds, so only road kill could explain the decline
questions.explanation: The road opened access for cats and weeds and caused road deaths, so predation, habitat degradation and mortality are combined. With several co-occurring threats, the data cannot single out one cause, and effective management tackles them together.

questions.stem: Two islands have equal species richness. Island P's mammal community is dominated by one introduced species; island Q has similar numbers of several native species. Which statement is correct?
options: The islands have equal species diversity because they have the same number of species
Island P has higher genetic diversity because introduced species carry more alleles
Island Q has higher species diversity because individuals are spread more evenly among species
Island P has higher species diversity because one species there is very abundant and successful
questions.explanation: Species diversity depends on evenness as well as richness. With the same richness, the island where individuals are spread evenly has higher diversity than the one dominated by a single species. Richness alone does not measure diversity.

questions.stem: Which human activity directly reduces genetic diversity within a population?
options: Planting a wildlife corridor that links two separate populations
Moving a few animals between populations to allow interbreeding
Protecting a large area of habitat that holds many breeding adults
Removing most individuals so that only a few survive to breed
questions.explanation: A severe reduction in numbers, a population bottleneck, means only the alleles of the few survivors pass on, so variation is lost. Corridors, translocations between populations and large protected habitats all help maintain genetic diversity.

questions.stem: Climate change threatens biodiversity mainly by:
options: removing all carbon dioxide that plants need for photosynthesis
stopping all rainfall so that every ecosystem becomes a desert
shifting conditions faster than many species can move or adapt
lowering average temperatures so that species freeze in winter
questions.explanation: Rising temperatures, changing rainfall and ocean warming alter habitats and the timing of biological events, and many species cannot shift their range or adapt fast enough. Climate change raises carbon dioxide rather than removing it.
